newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Iraq says near big deal with ENI unit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Iraq says near big deal with ENI unit.

text.p: Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said on Thursday that Iraq was close to signing an important oilfield deal with a unit of Italian energy group ENI.

The long-discussed deal would be the first in Iraq for ENI but a company source was less upbeat than Rasheed, saying the project could not go ahead until U.N. sanctions, imposed after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, were lifted.

Rasheed, who is visiting Rome for talks aimed at boosting economic relations, said he held discussions with ENI and hoped that a deal with its oil production and distribution unit Agip to develop the Nasiriya oilfield could be concluded swiftly.
"We have reached a very advanced stage. We hope to settle in the coming weeks," Rasheed told a news conference. "We are in almost full agreement."
Rasheed described the Nasiriya deal as "strategic cooperation" and a "partnership" and said Agip was planning to invest $2 billion to develop the field if the deal went ahead.
The concession would be valid for about 23 years and Rasheed said he expected production to reach 300,000 barrels per day (bpd) after around four years with annual revenue of $2 billion.
"The investment is near to two billion dollars. It is a very important oil field," he said.
The company source who said U.N. needed to be lifted before the project went ahead, said: "Negotiations have been going on for a while but there's still the embargo problem."
Rasheed was optimistic. "With a deal or contract there are always limitations...of course with the embargo it is more serious so you need to be more flexible," he said.

But he said it was a bilateral deal that was good for both sides, and he did not foresee problems. He said Iraq was also discussing a gas pipeline to Turkey, an oil pipeline to Jordan, upgrading of refineries and other projects with Agip.

Iraq, owner of the world's second largest oil reserves after Saudi Arabia, said this month 10 developments were up for grabs and talks were underway with companies from Canada, Malaysia, Australia, Italy, South Korea, Turkey, Indonesia and Algeria.
Russia's LUKoil has signed to develop the seven billion barrel West Qurna field.
Rasheed made clear that other would-be winners would need to show political support for the ending of sanctions.

"We have to find the right political climate," he said. "Priority will be given to those (countries) who took a positive attitude towards alleviating Iraqi suffering over the centuries and more recently," he said.
He appealed to Italy and others not to listen to pressure from Washington, which he said wanted President Saddam Hussein removed before sanctions could be lifted.

"The agony of the Iraqi people has escalated to such an extent that it has truly become a genocide in every definition of the word. There is absolutely no reason for the suffering to continue," he said.

Rasheed said he also expected to conclude a deal with China soon for Iraq's Ahdab oilfield development and to sign deals with French companies. Total SA and Elf Aquitaine have said they are in talks with Iraq.
Rasheed said Iraq was looking to deals with foreign companies to increase output capacity to six million bpd by exploiting massive unexplored reserves estimated by Baghdad at 214 billion barrels.
Current output capacity was 2.5 million bpd, compared with 3.5 million bpd before the Gulf War, he said.
